title: Two silos, one plot: A&E waits and delayed discharges
text:
NotePreparation notes, not a session writeup



These notes propose a dataset and question for a possible session. Nothing here is a decision by a group. The figures are the agent’s first drafts for a facilitator to react to, and are labelled as such. Drafted by Claude Opus 5.5 after a planning conversation about cross-silo analysis in NHS performance work, from Public Health Scotland open data.

title: Two silos, one plot: A&E waits and delayed discharges
text:
Why this question
Health-service analysts tend to work one silo at a time. Emergency department waiting times are published and analysed by one team, and delayed discharges by another. Ambulance handovers belong to a third. Each team’s output is a chart of its own measure.
But patient flow doesn’t respect those boundaries. A patient who is medically fit to leave hospital but can’t, because no care package or care-home place is ready, occupies a bed. If enough beds are occupied that way, patients admitted through A&E wait in the department for a bed, and the four-hour figure falls. Clinicians call this “exit block”. The causal story crosses two silos, so seeing it needs a chart that crosses them too.
Both halves are public. Public Health Scotland publishes monthly A&E activity and monthly delayed-discharge bed days, by health board, as open data. Those two datasets are rarely put on the same chart. That makes this a serious, topical question, not a toy, with open data and a clear grammar lesson.
The grammar lesson. In ggplot2, every layer can take its own data. A plot doesn’t have to begin with one tidy data frame. That’s a small point in the documentation, but here it carries weight: the language already supports cross-silo charts, so the analyst’s habit of starting from one table is what stands in the way. The session can test this directly, and also test where it goes wrong (see Three ways to put two silos on one plot).






TipReproducing this page





The data is cached in three files in data/, all from the Public Health Scotland open data portal, under the Open Government Licence v3:

phs-ae-monthly.csv: Monthly A&E activity and waiting times, one row per site, month and attendance category.
phs-delayed-discharge.csv: Delayed discharges in NHSScotland, bed days by health board, month, age group and reason.
phs-health-boards.csv: Health board codes and labels.

The cached pull was made on 2026-10-09 and runs to August 2026. The download URLs carry the release month, so a refresh needs the current URLs from each dataset page:

  readr::write_csv("data/phs-ae-monthly.csv")

  readr::write_csv("data/phs-delayed-discharge.csv")

title: Two silos, one plot: A&E waits and delayed discharges
text:
What’s in the two silos

A&E. 40,066 rows, one per site, month and attendance category, from July 2007 to August 2026. Sites are either Type 1 (emergency departments) or Type 3 (minor injury units). The four-hour standard means the most at Type 1 sites, so this page keeps only those and sums them to board level, giving 14 boards with an emergency department.
Delayed discharges. 27,450 rows, one per board (plus a Scotland total), month, age group and reason for delay, from July 2016. The measure is bed days lost to delays and the average number of beds occupied each day. This page uses adults (18 and over), all reasons.
The shared keys are health board of treatment (HBT, the same 2019 codes in both) and month. The months are stored as numbers like 202608. The repository’s describe script reads them as continuous numbers, which they aren’t: 201612 to 201701 looks like a jump of 89. Parsing them as dates is the first step for any time axis.
The overlap is 122 months, July 2016 to August 2026. The A&E series goes back further, but the delayed-discharge series on the portal starts in July 2016. An older series to June 2016 is published separately, and this page hasn’t checked whether the two are comparable.

title: Two silos, one plot: A&E waits and delayed discharges
text:
First drafts of the figures
These are the agent’s drafts, made without a group. Each one is a set of decisions the group can overturn.

The silo view: two charts, one above the other


Code
covid <- annotate("rect", xmin = ymd("2020-03-01"), xmax = ymd("2021-03-01"),
                  ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.12)

p_ae <- ggplot(both_scot, aes(month, pct_4h)) +
  covid +
  geom_line(colour = "#0072B2") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Seen within 4 hours",
       title = "Emergency departments: share seen within four hours") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_dd <- ggplot(both_scot, aes(month, delayed_beds)) +
  covid +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Beds a day",
       title = "Hospital beds occupied by delayed discharges") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_ae / p_dd








Figure 1: Scotland, monthly. Each measure on its own, as its own team would publish it. The shaded band marks the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic.





Read one above the other, the two lines look like mirror images. In July 2016 emergency departments saw 95% of patients within four hours, while delayed discharges took up 1,417 beds a day. By August 2026 the figures were 62% and 1,971. The pandemic year breaks the pattern in an informative way: delays fell sharply, and four-hour performance briefly recovered with them.
This is how most readers meet the two measures, and it already hints at the relationship. But it asks the reader to do the cross-silo work by eye.


The cross-silo view: one measure against the other


Code
both_scot |>
  ggplot(aes(delayed_beds, pct_4h, colour = month)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(trans = "date", labels = scales::label_date("%Y")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Beds occupied by delayed discharges (daily average)",
       y = "A&E patients seen within 4 hours", colour = NULL,
       title = "More delayed beds, longer A&E waits") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm"), legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 2: Scotland, monthly, one point per month joined in time order. Colour runs from the earliest month (dark) to the latest (yellow).





This is the same grammar as the Rosling trails on the gapminder page: two measures on x and y, and time carried by the path and the colour. Across the 122 months the correlation is -0.87.
That number needs care. Look inside the dark cluster of pre-pandemic months: it has almost no slope. Most of the correlation comes from the shift between eras, before 2020 and after 2021, not from months with more delays having worse waits. Both series trend over the decade, and almost any two trending series would correlate this strongly. The chart is evidence that the two silos belong on one chart, not evidence that one causes the other. Separating the trend from the month-to-month link is the next question, and probably a session of its own.


The board view: does every board show it?


Code
both_hb |>
  ggplot(aes(delayed_beds, pct_4h, alpha = month)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.9, colour = "#0072B2") +
  facet_wrap(~ board, scales = "free_x", ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 4) +
  scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.1, 0.9), trans = "date", guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Beds occupied by delayed discharges (daily average)",
       y = "A&E patients seen within 4 hours",
       title = "The pattern, board by board") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(1.5, "lines"))








Figure 3: Each health board with an emergency department, one point per month, older months fainter. The x scales are free because boards differ hugely in size.





The board panels are where the group’s domain knowledge matters most. A board where the cloud slopes clearly down is consistent with exit block. A board where it doesn’t is the more interesting case: is it a small island board with few delays to begin with, or a board that kept A&E flowing despite the delays? The data can raise that question but not answer it.
A first look already shows that the boards don’t all tell the Scotland story. Ayrshire and Arran, Forth Valley and Greater Glasgow and Clyde slope down much as Scotland does. In Lanarkshire and Lothian, the recent months sit lower than the early ones without sitting further right: A&E performance fell while delays didn’t rise, so something other than delayed discharges moved. In Orkney and Shetland, delayed beds are counted in single figures and the points fall into vertical stripes. There, a single patient is a visible step on the x axis.

title: Two silos, one plot: A&E waits and delayed discharges
section: Three ways to put two silos on one plot
text:
Three ways to put two silos on one plot
The session’s grammar exercise is to build the cross-silo chart three ways and compare them.
1. Vectors from two data frames. ggplot2 accepts aes(x = delays_scot$delayed_beds, y = ed_scot$pct_4h). This feels like the most direct expression of “this silo against that one”, and it needs no join. It’s also the fragile one. It pairs rows by position, not by month. The two series here start in different years (230 A&E months and 122 delay months), so this errors, which is the lucky outcome. If the lengths happened to match while the months didn’t, it would draw a wrong chart with no warning.


Code
# Fragile: pairs rows by position, not by month
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = delays_scot$delayed_beds, y = ed_scot$pct_4h))


2. Each layer with its own data. For the time-series view, each line can be its own layer with its own data, as in the silo figures above. This works whenever the layers share axes, and it is the honest version of “one plot, several silos”. It can’t make a scatter of one silo against the other, because a point needs both values in one row.
3. Join on the shared keys, then plot. inner_join(ed_scot, delays_scot, by = "month") is what this page does. The join makes the pairing rule explicit and checkable: the same board, the same month. It also drops months that only one silo has, and the validator can check what was dropped.
The comparison is the lesson. The grammar allows all three. Choosing between them is about how errors are kept out, and that is the validator’s job, not the coder’s.

title: Two silos, one plot: A&E waits and delayed discharges
text:
Candidate mappings (the group chooses)
Candidates (the group chooses) - nhs-cross-silo:
  joined grain:   board x month (14 boards with an ED, Jul 2016 - Aug 2026)
  position x/y:   pct_4h (A&E), delayed_beds (delays), month (time)
  time:           month - as x, as path order, as colour, or as alpha
  facet:          board (14) - free scales needed; or year
  colour:         year or season (winter vs rest) - not board (too many)
  size:           attendances (board size) - but it dominates, as population did in gapminder
  other silos:    attendances (demand), delay reason (health/social care vs Code 9)
Questions for the group:

Rates or counts? Delayed beds are a count, and boards differ in size by an order of magnitude. Beds per 100,000 adults would need a third, population, silo.
Season. Winter pressure moves both measures together. Colour by season, or facet by year, to see whether the link holds outside winter.
The third silo. Ambulance handover times would complete the chain from front door to back door. They aren’t on the Public Health Scotland open data portal (as of 2026-10-09 the only ambulance dataset there is from a COVID-19 wider-impacts series). Finding a public source is a task worth setting before the session.

title: Two silos, one plot: A&E waits and delayed discharges
text:
What the data can’t say
These are monthly board totals, so they can’t follow a patient. They can’t show that the person waiting in A&E was waiting for the bed that a delayed patient occupied. Both measures share drivers, such as an ageing population, winter, the pandemic and staffing, that could move them together without one causing the other. The four-hour figure counts all Type 1 attendances, including the majority who are never admitted and so never need a ward bed. A cleaner test would use admitted patients only, and that breakdown isn’t in this file. The delayed-discharge figures come from a monthly census and bed-day returns, with definitions set nationally. A change in what counts as a delay would show up as a change in the line. Finally, the joined record covers about ten years, which includes one pandemic and very few independent “experiments”.

title: The Office: what’s in the data
section: A first figure: ratings by season and episode
text:
A first figure: ratings by season and episode
The first spec asked for a heatmap: season as rows, episode number as columns, and IMDb rating as fill. Everything else is left at ggplot2’s defaults.
# sessions/2026-09-29/specs/01-office-heatmap.yml
data: tt-2020-03-17-office_ratings
mapping:
  x: episode
  y: season
  fill: imdb_rating
layers:
  - geom: tile


Code
ggplot(ratings, aes(x = episode, y = season, fill = imdb_rating)) +
  geom_tile() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 1





Looking at the render shows three defaults that nobody decided on:

season is stored as a number, so ggplot2 treats it as continuous. The axis shows breaks at 2.5, 5.0 and 7.5, which are seasons that don’t exist.
The default continuous y scale puts season 1 at the bottom and season 9 at the top.
The default fill gradient runs from dark to light blue, which leaves little contrast across the 6.7–9.7 range.

The ragged right edge shows how many episodes each season had. Season 1 is the shortest, with 6 episodes.

title: The Office: what’s in the data
section: A second figure: ratings over air date
text:
A second figure: ratings over air date
The second spec puts each episode at its air date, colours it by season, and adds a smoother. Two decisions were made before compiling:

Season as a category. season is stored as a number, so the spec maps factor(season) to colour, which gives one hue per season instead of a gradient. Shape was dropped: ggplot2’s default shape palette has only six shapes, so seasons 7–9 would have gone missing.
One smoother per season. Colour is mapped for the whole plot, so the smooth layer inherits it and fits a separate curve to each season.

# sessions/2026-09-29/specs/02-office-airdate.yml
data: tt-2020-03-17-office_ratings
mapping:
  x: air_date
  y: imdb_rating
  colour: factor(season)
layers:
  - geom: point
  - geom: smooth


Code
ggplot(ratings, aes(x = air_date, y = imdb_rating, colour = factor(season))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 2





Looking at the render:

The smoother defaults to loess, which is very wiggly when seasons are this short (a median of 23 episodes). Season 1’s 6 episodes give a spike with no confidence ribbon, and R prints a warning while fitting it.
Season 4’s ribbon balloons across a gap in its air dates. Loess is drawing a curve through months with no episodes.
Several seasons end on a rise, most sharply the finale at 9.7. A flexible smoother bends towards the last point or two, so these end-of-season spikes need checking against the raw points before reading anything into them.
The legend title is the code factor(season), and the axis titles are raw variable names, because the spec has no labs block yet.

title: The Office: what’s in the data
text:
What the data can’t say
IMDb ratings come from self-selected raters voting years after broadcast, so they measure how the show is remembered by people who chose to rate it. They don’t measure how it was received at the time. The episode counts also differ between tables (188 rated episodes against 186 in the transcripts). The sources likely split two-part episodes differently. Check any join for dropped rows. The transcripts are fan-made, so character labels are inconsistent: the same person can appear under several spellings, which inflates the character count.

title: The Office: what’s in the data
text:
Reflections on in-person/hybrid session

Some people had preference for something more GUI/point-and-click rather than the dev-style IDE presented.

My discussion about text-based ragged data structures, like the YAML/JSON-like universal gg specification offered in the gg-spec skill, might have been too close to the bedrock on average.

Less resistance to CC/Codex taking over implementation tasks than I was expecting.
Soft support for key argument made: that more of analysts/analytical knowledge workers’ time should be spent on the design decisions.

e.g. I mentioned ggplot2 used to have qplot, but the defaults took too many important design decisions from the user, so was deprecated.
This is now the ‘stuff to sweat’, though maybe a gui will help even more

Less continual iteration over specific visualisation. Didn’t get to show committing as like rappeling in rock climbing, and this being an organic process.

Next steps:

Get workbook at the end of the session committed and rendered as a page on github pages for showing to attendees.
Get a second version of the workshop doc with incremental improvements to visualisation also shown, along with a ‘wow’ visualisation’, such as a 3D plot, and something generated by Opus 5.5 autonomously.
Produce a skill with replicates a tableau-style gui way of specifying mapping from dataset features to visual aesthetics in a ggplot2 way. Have this as another page along with some ready datasets to select from.
Contextualise what the workshop showed as one key aspect of one of the three modules I’m developing for the Knowledge Tree collection, namely ‘Science Supercharged’. Give links and a description to the broader package and illustrative savings in total time through collapsing of implementation time.

title: One mapping line, two opposite conclusions
text:
TipNot a session page — a demonstration



This page shows the working method the sessions use: a plot is specified as a short YAML document of grammar-of-graphics mapping rules, the spec is compiled to ggplot2 code, the figure is rendered and looked at, and what looking reveals drives the next revision of the spec. How these sessions work.
In a live session, nobody types ggplot2 code to begin with. The group dictates mapping rules — which variable goes to which aesthetic, which geoms draw them, which scales transform them — and those rules are written down as a spec. The spec is short enough to argue about on a shared screen, and it is the record of the design decisions that ends up quoted in the writeup.
Here is one full round trip on the Palmer penguins data.
Code
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(!is.na(bill_depth_mm))

slope_pooled <- coef(lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins))[2]
slopes_species <- penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  group_modify(~ tibble(slope = coef(lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = .x))[2])) |>
  ungroup()

title: One mapping line, two opposite conclusions
section: Round 1: the spec as first dictated
text:
Round 1: the spec as first dictated
The group asks a simple question — do penguins with longer bills also have deeper bills? — and dictates the minimal spec: two positional mappings, points, and a linear trend.
# Worked example, round 1 — compiled in example-gg-spec.qmd
data: penguins
filter: "!is.na(bill_depth_mm)"
mapping:
  x: bill_length_mm
  y: bill_depth_mm
layers:
  - geom: point
    alpha: 0.6
  - geom: smooth
    stat: lm
    se: true
labs:
  title: "Do longer bills mean deeper bills?"
  subtitle: "342 penguins, Palmer Archipelago 2007-09"
  x: "Bill length (mm)"
  y: "Bill depth (mm)"
theme: minimal
The spec compiles to code a reader could have written by hand — layers in spec order, nothing the spec didn’t ask for:


Code
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Do longer bills mean deeper bills?",
    subtitle = sprintf("%d penguins, Palmer Archipelago 2007-09", nrow(penguins)),
    x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)"
  )








Figure 1: Round 1: bill depth against bill length, all penguins pooled. The fitted line slopes down.

title: One mapping line, two opposite conclusions
text:
Looking at the render
The fitted line says no: pooled across all 342 birds, each extra millimetre of bill length goes with 0.085 mm less depth. That contradicts any intuition about bigger birds having bigger bills — and looking at the point cloud shows why the line is suspect: the points sit in distinct clumps the spec has done nothing to distinguish.
The group’s diagnosis, in grammar terms: a variable that structures the data has been left out of the mapping. The fix is one line.

title: One mapping line, two opposite conclusions
text:
Round 2: one mapping line added
# Worked example, round 2 — one mapping line added: colour: species
data: penguins
filter: "!is.na(bill_depth_mm)"
mapping:
  x: bill_length_mm
  y: bill_depth_mm
  colour: species
layers:
  - geom: point
    alpha: 0.6
  - geom: smooth
    stat: lm
    se: true
scales:
  colour: okabe-ito
labs:
  title: "Within every species, the slope reverses"
  subtitle: "The same 342 penguins, now mapped by species"
  x: "Bill length (mm)"
  y: "Bill depth (mm)"
  colour: "Species"
theme: minimal
Only colour: species (and a colour-blind-safe scale for it) has been added. But because geom_smooth inherits the plot-level mapping, colour doesn’t just tint the points — it groups the stat, and one regression becomes three.


Code
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(palette.colors(3, palette = "Okabe-Ito"))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Within every species, the slope reverses",
    subtitle = sprintf("The same %d penguins, now mapped by species", nrow(penguins)),
    x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)", colour = "Species"
  )








Figure 2: Round 2: the same data with species mapped to colour. Within every species the slope is positive.





Within each species the relationship runs the way intuition says it should — slopes of 0.18, 0.22, 0.20 mm per mm for Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo respectively, every one positive. The pooled negative slope was Simpson’s paradox: Gentoos are long-billed but shallow-billed, and pooling let the between-species contrast masquerade as a within-penguin trend.

title: One mapping line, two opposite conclusions
text:
What the round trip teaches

Mappings are decisions. The difference between the two figures — and two opposite conclusions — is a single line in the spec. Leaving a variable out of the mapping is as much a choice as putting it in.
Aesthetics reach further than appearance. Mapping colour regrouped the statistical layer, not just the ink. In the grammar, mappings feed stats, not only geoms.
The render is part of the method. The clumpy point cloud was visible in Round 1’s figure but nowhere in its spec or code. You find it by looking.

title: One mapping line, two opposite conclusions
text:
What the data can’t say
Three species from three islands over three seasons cannot separate species from island effects (Chinstraps and Gentoos were each sampled on effectively one island), and a within-species slope across individuals is still not a growth trajectory — no penguin was measured twice. The paradox here is a lesson about mappings, not a finding about penguins.

title: Agentic data-vis workshops
text:
Occasional, hands-on workshops on data visualisation with an agentic AI assistant, grounded in Wilkinson’s grammar of graphics. The work is mainly in R with ggplot2, with excursions into Vega-Lite and plotnine to show the grammar moving between languages. Each session takes one TidyTuesday (or equivalent) dataset and builds a visualisation live. Every design decision is made by the people in the room. The agent fetches and describes the data, writes the code, renders the result, and reports what it sees.
There’s no fixed schedule. Sessions happen when someone offers to run one, and the repo is public so that anyone can: clone it, open it in an IDE with Claude Code, Codex, or another coding agent, and the same skills and instructions apply. Started by Jon Minton.

title: Agentic data-vis workshops
text:
How the sessions work
Plots are specified before they are coded. The group dictates mapping rules: which variable goes to which aesthetic, which geoms, which scales. These are recorded in a short YAML spec that the group argues over on the shared screen, then compiled to code and rendered. The spec trail is the record of the design decisions. See a worked example of the round trip.
For anyone who would rather point and click than write YAML, the mapping builder lets you draw the same mapping rules as arrows from variables to aesthetics. It shows the figure, the spec and the ggplot2 code updating together.
The opposite of “the analyst decides” is an agent that decides everything: the dataset, the question and every figure. That is the claude-fable-vision-ds-test experiment (repository), which these workshops use as a point of contrast. Its probability-phrases page covers one of the datasets offered in Session 1.
The repo gives the agent three skills, each a plain-markdown procedure that any agent can follow:

tt-fetch fetches a TidyTuesday week and describes it in grammar terms. It proposes mappings and never chooses one.
gg-spec compiles a YAML spec to ggplot2, renders it, and looks at the result. It walks the grammar one slot at a time, so the room makes each decision.
dataset-scout finds datasets that stress a particular grammar layer, for planning a session.

After a session, a page may be drafted from the spec trail and notes, recording the design decisions as decisions, the pain points, and the lessons learned. The session’s facilitator reviews and approves it before it is published.

title: Agentic data-vis workshops
text:
Consent and authorship
The Chatham House Rule applies by default: write-ups never attribute a view or a mistake to an individual. Participants who consent may be named as contributors, which needs a per-session consent record: no record, no name. Recordings and transcripts, if any, are never published.

section: A first figure: ratings by season and episode
text:
A first figure: ratings by season and episode
The first spec asked for a heatmap: season as rows, episode number as columns, and IMDb rating as fill. Everything else is left at ggplot2’s defaults.
# sessions/2026-09-29/specs/01-office-heatmap.yml
data: tt-2020-03-17-office_ratings
mapping:
  x: episode
  y: season
  fill: imdb_rating
layers:
  - geom: tile


Code
ggplot(ratings, aes(x = episode, y = season, fill = imdb_rating)) +
  geom_tile() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 1





Looking at the render shows three defaults that nobody decided on:

season is stored as a number, so ggplot2 treats it as continuous. The axis shows breaks at 2.5, 5.0 and 7.5, which are seasons that don’t exist.
The default continuous y scale puts season 1 at the bottom and season 9 at the top.
The default fill gradient runs from dark to light blue, which leaves little contrast across the 6.7–9.7 range.

The ragged right edge shows how many episodes each season had. Season 1 is the shortest, with 6 episodes.

title: The Office: what’s in the data, version 2
section: A second figure: ratings over air date
text:
A second figure: ratings over air date
The second spec puts each episode at its air date, colours it by season, and adds a smoother. Two decisions were made before compiling:

Season as a category. season is stored as a number, so the spec maps factor(season) to colour, which gives one hue per season instead of a gradient. Shape was dropped: ggplot2’s default shape palette has only six shapes, so seasons 7–9 would have gone missing.
One smoother per season. Colour is mapped for the whole plot, so the smooth layer inherits it and fits a separate curve to each season.

# sessions/2026-09-29/specs/02-office-airdate.yml
data: tt-2020-03-17-office_ratings
mapping:
  x: air_date
  y: imdb_rating
  colour: factor(season)
layers:
  - geom: point
  - geom: smooth


Code
ggplot(ratings, aes(x = air_date, y = imdb_rating, colour = factor(season))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 2





Looking at the render:

The smoother defaults to loess, which is very wiggly when seasons are this short (a median of 23 episodes). Season 1’s 6 episodes give a spike with no confidence ribbon, and R prints a warning while fitting it.
Season 4’s ribbon balloons across a gap in its air dates. Loess is drawing a curve through months with no episodes.
Several seasons end on a rise, most sharply the finale at 9.7. A flexible smoother bends towards the last point or two, so these end-of-season spikes need checking against the raw points before reading anything into them.
The legend title is the code factor(season), and the axis titles are raw variable names, because the spec has no labs block yet.

text:
Revisions to the first two figures
The facilitator reviewed what the renders had revealed and made these decisions:

Season is a category, not a cardinal number. Season 3 isn’t “three times” season 1.
Season 1 goes at the top, so the heatmap reads like a table.
The fill uses viridis for more contrast across the ratings.
Per-season smoothers become straight lines (method: lm).
A second version shows one smoother for the whole series.
Every figure gets proper labels.

       x = "Episode within season", y = "Season", fill = "IMDb rating") +

Figure 3





With season as a category, each row is one season and the axis shows only seasons that exist. scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) puts season 1 at the top. Viridis runs from dark purple to yellow, so the season 8 slump and the high points stand out. The finale is the brightest tile in the last row.


Spec 04: one straight line per season

  x: air_date
  y: imdb_rating
  colour: factor(season)

  - geom: smooth
    method: lm

  x: "Original air date"
  y: "IMDb rating"
  colour: "Season"


Code

  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(title = "Ratings over the run, with a linear trend per season",
       x = "Original air date", y = "IMDb rating", colour = "Season") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 4





geom_smooth(method = "lm") runs a regression that doesn’t appear anywhere in the code. For each season, ggplot2 fits lm(imdb_rating ~ air_date) to that season’s episodes and draws the fitted line with a 95% confidence band. The straight lines are far steadier than the loess curves of the first version. Season 4’s line now crosses its gap in air dates without bending. That gap is still worth knowing about: a line drawn through months with no episodes claims nothing about them.


Spec 05: one smoother for the whole series
This spec uses a feature that was added to the gg-spec schema for it: a layer-level mapping. Colour is mapped on the point layer only, so the smooth layer no longer inherits it and fits one curve to all 188 episodes.
# sessions/2026-09-29/specs/05-office-airdate-pooled.yml
data: tt-2020-03-17-office_ratings
mapping:
  x: air_date
  y: imdb_rating
layers:
  - geom: point
    mapping:
      colour: factor(season)
  - geom: smooth
labs:
  title: "Ratings over the run, with one smoother for the whole series"
  x: "Original air date"
  y: "IMDb rating"
  colour: "Season"


Code
ggplot(ratings, aes(x = air_date, y = imdb_rating)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = factor(season))) +
  geom_smooth() +
  labs(title = "Ratings over the run, with one smoother for the whole series",
       x = "Original air date", y = "IMDb rating", colour = "Season") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 5





Moving one colour mapping from the plot level to the point layer changes the question the figure answers. Spec 04 asks how ratings move within a season. Spec 05 asks how they move across the whole run: up to a peak in seasons 3 and 4, then down. With 188 points, loess is no longer too flexible.

title: The Office: what’s in the data, version 2
section: A 3D view, with the models made explicit
text:
A 3D view, with the models made explicit


Code
# Within-season lines: season as a category, with its own intercept and slope.
# This parameterisation gives each season's intercept and slope directly.
m_lines <- lm(imdb_rating ~ 0 + factor(season) + factor(season):episode, data = ratings)

# Across-season planes: season as a cardinal number.
m_plane <- lm(imdb_rating ~ episode + season, data = ratings)   # flat plane
m_twist <- lm(imdb_rating ~ episode * season, data = ratings)   # twisted plane

r2 <- \(m) sprintf("%.2f", summary(m)$r.squared)

# Comparable R² for the within-season model: refit it with an intercept (same fitted
# values, same residuals) so R² is measured against the mean rating, not against zero.
r2_lines <- summary(lm(imdb_rating ~ factor(season) * episode, data = ratings))$r.squared


Rating is elevation, episode is x and season is y. Use the buttons to add one of three linear models. The table alongside updates to show the model behind the surface, its lm() call, and its coefficients. Drag to rotate the view, and scroll to zoom.
Seen from straight above, this is the heatmap again, with rating as height instead of colour.
The buttons offer two kinds of model:

Within-season lines treat season as a category, as the facilitator decided. Each season gets its own intercept and slope, so this is the model that spec 04’s geom_smooth(method = "lm") fits implicitly. The one difference is that x here is episode number, where spec 04 used air date.
Across-season planes treat season as a cardinal number. That goes against the decision above, and it has to: a plane needs a continuous y. Season becomes a quantity, and the model assumes each season shifts the rating by the same amount as the one before.

The flat plane adds episode and season effects.
The twisted plane adds their interaction, so the within-season slope changes steadily from season to season.


Comparing the fits shows the cost of that assumption. The plane explains 0.18 of the variance in ratings, and the twisted plane 0.19. The nine separate lines explain 0.46, but they use 18 parameters to do it.

section: From a lead to an ensemble (autonomous)
text:
From a lead to an ensemble (autonomous)






ImportantProduced autonomously by Claude Opus 5.5



For this section the facilitator asked only for “something with the transcripts”. The agent chose the question, the measures, the figures and every design decision in them, so none of them was decided by the facilitator or the session group. This is the contrast case described on the home page. Its fuller form, where an agent picks the dataset as well, is the claude-fable-vision-ds-test experiment (repository).




Code
lines_clean <- lines |> mutate(character = str_squish(character))
episodes <- lines_clean |>
  distinct(season, episode, imdb_rating) |>
  arrange(season, episode) |>
  mutate(ep_seq = row_number())

shares <- lines_clean |>
  count(season, episode, character) |>
  group_by(season, episode) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

leads <- c("Michael", "Dwight", "Jim", "Pam", "Andy")
lead_shares <- shares |>
  mutate(who = if_else(character %in% leads, character, "everyone else")) |>
  group_by(season, episode, who) |>
  summarise(share = sum(share), .groups = "drop") |>
  complete(nesting(season, episode), who, fill = list(share = 0)) |>
  left_join(episodes, by = c("season", "episode")) |>
  mutate(who = factor(who, levels = c(leads, "everyone else")))

# Effective number of speakers: the inverse Simpson index of line shares.
# One speaker with every line scores 1; ten speakers with equal shares score 10.
breadth <- shares |>
  group_by(season, episode) |>
  summarise(eff_speakers = 1 / sum(share^2), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(episodes, by = c("season", "episode"))

eff_by_season <- breadth |> group_by(season) |> summarise(eff = mean(eff_speakers))
michael_by_season <- lead_shares |> filter(who == "Michael") |>
  group_by(season) |> summarise(share = mean(share))

pooled   <- lm(imdb_rating ~ eff_speakers, data = breadth)
within   <- lm(imdb_rating ~ eff_speakers + factor(season), data = breadth)
pooled_r <- cor(breadth$eff_speakers, breadth$imdb_rating)
season_starts <- episodes |> group_by(season) |> summarise(start = min(ep_seq))


The question the agent chose. The Office started as a show about one man and became an ensemble. Can the transcripts measure that shift? And does a broader ensemble go with better or worse ratings?
In season 1, Michael speaks 33% of all lines in an average episode. By season 7, his last as a regular, that has fallen to 20%. The effective number of speakers is the number of equally talkative characters that would give an episode’s spread of lines. It rises from 5.2 in season 1 to 10.6 in season 9.


Code
ggplot(lead_shares, aes(x = ep_seq, y = share, fill = who)) +
  geom_area(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_vline(data = season_starts[-1, ], aes(xintercept = start - 0.5),
             colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(unname(palette.colors(6, palette = "Okabe-Ito"))[c(6, 2, 3, 4, 5)], "grey80")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = season_starts$start, labels = paste0("S", season_starts$season),
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Who speaks: share of each episode's lines",
       x = "Episode, in broadcast order (season starts marked)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")








Figure 7





Design choices (the agent’s).

It used a stacked area of shares, not counts, because episodes differ in length and the question is about balance.
The five leads are named and everyone else is pooled in grey. The transcripts have hundreds of character labels, and colour can’t carry them.
Okabe-Ito hues keep the leads distinguishable for colour-blind readers.
White rules mark the season boundaries, and the x-axis labels sit at season starts instead of at arbitrary episode numbers.



Code
ggplot(breadth, aes(x = eff_speakers, y = imdb_rating)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = factor(season)), alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = factor(season)), method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey20", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Broader ensembles, lower ratings? Only between seasons",
       x = "Effective number of speakers in the episode", y = "IMDb rating",
       colour = "Season", caption = "Dashed: one line through all episodes. Solid: one line per season.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 8





Pooled across the whole run, the effective number of speakers and the rating are negatively correlated (r = -0.26). Each extra effective speaker goes with a rating 0.06 points lower. Give each season its own level, with lm(imdb_rating ~ eff_speakers + factor(season)), and the common within-season slope is +0.02 per extra speaker (p = 0.35), which is indistinguishable from zero. The nine season lines in the figure scatter both ways around it, with no consistent direction.
The pooled slope comes from between-season differences. The later seasons both spread their lines more widely and are rated lower. Nothing in the data shows that one causes the other. Michael’s departure after season 7, cast and writing-staff changes, and the age of the show all shift ratings and ensemble breadth together.
The grammar point. The same move as spec 04 against spec 05 changes the answer: one smoother, or one per group, chosen by where a single mapping sits. With group-level confounding, the choice of layer decides whether the figure supports the claim.

title: The Office: what’s in the data, version 2
text:
Where this fits
The workshop’s central argument is that agents collapse the implementation part of analysis, which leaves the analyst more time for the design decisions. Knowledge Tree and Butterfly, the facilitator’s company, is building this into its offering Science Supercharged. It brings the habits software teams use to keep their work alive to research analysis: version control, specification before analysis, and checks before publication. The spec-first loop in these sessions is a small, visual instance of that. The decisions go into a file that can be reviewed, an agent does the typing, and the record of what was decided survives the session.
The knowledge tree explains the wider idea: keep alive the structure that produces an analysis, not just the outputs. The 75-second film A Hand of Tasks frames the shift in four task types: specify, implement, review and feedback. Sessions like this one practise moving time out of implement and into the other three.
How much time is at stake? Illustrative orders of magnitude, not measurements. These estimates are deliberately low.








Piece of work
By hand, experienced R user
Agent-assisted (human time)




One spec revision to a polished, labelled figure
10–30 minutes
about 1 minute


This page’s figures, including the 3D model view and its linked table
1–2 days
1–2 hours


Rebuilding a published paper’s analysis on new data (Science Supercharged case study)
weeks
2–3 days



The saving is roughly an order of magnitude on implementation. Specifying, reviewing and deciding take as long as before, which is the point.

title: The Office: what’s in the data, version 2
text:
What the data can’t say
IMDb ratings come from self-selected raters voting years after broadcast, so they measure how the show is remembered by people who chose to rate it. They don’t measure how it was received at the time.
The episode counts differ between tables (188 rated episodes against 186 in the transcripts). The sources likely split two-part episodes differently. Check any join for dropped rows.
The transcripts are fan-made, so character labels are inconsistent. The effective-speaker measure counts lines, not words or screen time, so a character with many one-word lines counts as much as one with a few speeches.
The 3D planes assume season acts as a number, which the group rejected for the 2D figures. They are shown to make that assumption, and its cost, visible.

title: Global fertility: what’s in the data
text:
NotePreparation notes, not a session writeup



These notes describe a candidate dataset before any session. The group has made no design decisions. The two Rosling-style figures were asked for by the facilitator as a familiar reference point, and the candidate mappings at the end are options for the group to choose from. Drafted by Claude Opus 5.5 from the output of scripts/describe_data.R and the Rdatasets documentation for dslabs::gapminder.
The data is the gapminder table from Rafael Irizarry’s dslabs package, which compiles Gapminder country indicators. It has one row per country per year, giving each country’s total fertility rate (births per woman) alongside life expectancy, infant mortality, population and GDP.

title: Global fertility: what’s in the data
text:
Reading it

What it is. Country indicators compiled by Gapminder, covering 185 countries from 1960 to 2016.
Grain. One row per country per year, 10,545 rows. There’s no reshaping to do: the data is already tidy.
Types in grammar terms. fertility, life_expectancy, infant_mortality, population and gdp are continuous. year is temporal and works as a continuous x. continent (5 levels) is the only discrete variable in the range for colour or facets; region (22) and country have too many levels for either.
Missingness has a shape. gdp is 28.2% missing. It stops after 2011 and is patchy before 1980. fertility (1.8% missing) and infant_mortality (13.8%) have no values at all for 2016, so in practice the fertility series ends in 2015. A line plot that runs to 2016 will stop short without warning.
Range. Fertility runs from 0.84 (Macao, China, 2003) to 9.22 (Yemen, 1983).

title: Global fertility: what’s in the data
text:
Rosling-style reference figures
Anyone who watched Hans Rosling’s talks will recognise these: fertility on x, life expectancy on y, one bubble per country sized by population and coloured by continent. They are here as a shared starting point to react to, not as the group’s choices. The facilitator asked for them in preparation, and the group can keep, change or throw away any slot.
The animated original shows time by moving the bubbles. A static page has to put time somewhere else, and the two figures below make that choice in two different ways.


Code
decades <- seq(1960, 2010, by = 10)

rosling <- gm |>
  filter(!is.na(fertility), !is.na(life_expectancy), !is.na(population))

continent_cols <- c(Africa = "#E69F00", Americas = "#D55E00", Asia = "#009E73",
                    Europe = "#0072B2", Oceania = "#CC79A7") # Okabe-Ito



Time as facets: one panel per decade


Code
rosling |>
  filter(year %in% decades) |>
  arrange(desc(population)) |> # draw big bubbles first so small ones stay visible
  ggplot(aes(x = fertility, y = life_expectancy,
             size = population, colour = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = continent_cols) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Total fertility rate (births per woman, reversed)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Fewer children, longer lives, 1960 to 2010") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 1: Each panel is one year at the start of a decade. Read across the panels to see the cloud of countries move from top left to bottom right.





The x axis is reversed, which is a decision to argue about. Reversed, the movement over time runs left to right, and “fewer births” sits on the same side as “longer lives”. Rosling himself plotted fertility the natural way round (high on the right), so the countries moved right to left. Neither is wrong. But the choice changes what readers see as progress.
Two figures from the data anchor the panels. In 1960 the median country had 6.19 births per woman and a life expectancy of 56.3; by 2010 those medians were 2.38 and 73.6.


Time as fading: older years more transparent


Code
latest <- rosling |> filter(year == max(year))

rosling |>
  arrange(country, year) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fertility, y = life_expectancy, colour = continent)) +
  geom_path(aes(group = country, alpha = year), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(data = latest, aes(size = population), alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.03, 0.6), guide = "none") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = continent_cols) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Total fertility rate (births per woman, reversed)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)", colour = NULL,
       title = paste0("Where each country came from, ", min(rosling$year),
                      " to ", max(rosling$year))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 2: Each country’s path from 1960 to 2015, fading into the past. The solid bubbles are the latest year with fertility data.





This version uses alpha for time, so older data is more faded. It keeps the movement in one panel, but the paths overlap heavily, and the faint tails are hard to read for any single country. Note the two layers here: the trails use all 10,358 rows, and the bubbles use a second data frame of only the latest year. That every layer can take its own data is itself a grammar point. It comes back on the cross-silo page.
Looking at the rendered figures shows things the code doesn’t. The few sudden vertical drops in life expectancy are not data errors. They are catastrophes: the large Asian bubble low in the 1960 panel is China (life expectancy 30.53) during the famine that followed the Great Leap Forward, and the lone Americas point low in the 2010 panel is Haiti (32.2) in the year of its earthquake. The trails show the same events as spikes.
Questions these two figures leave for the group:

Facets or alpha? Facets give clean snapshots but lose each country’s identity across panels. Alpha keeps identity and loses legibility.
Size. Bubble area tracks population, so China and India dominate every panel. Is that the right emphasis for a question about typical countries?
The stat. Both figures show raw points. A per-continent median path (a stat_summary layer) would be the geoms-and-stats lesson in one line of code.

title: Global fertility: what’s in the data
text:
What the data can’t say
These are national averages, so variation within a country is invisible, and every country counts equally whatever its population. The 1960s values for many countries are Gapminder’s estimates and interpolations, not registered births. The record also ends before the recent falls in fertility.

title: Global fertility: what’s in the data
text:
Candidate mappings (the group chooses)
Candidates (the group chooses) - gapminder-fertility:
  position x/y (continuous): fertility, life_expectancy, infant_mortality (14% NA),
                             population, gdp (28% NA, ends 2011)
  time:                      year (continuous, 1960-2015 usable for fertility)
  colour / facet (5 levels): continent
  size:                      population (spans 5 orders of magnitude)
  not for colour:            region (22), country (185) - filter or highlight a few
Why the data could suit geoms and stats: if you map year to x and fertility to y, you get 10,358 points, and those points can be drawn as dots, as one line per country, as a smoother per continent, or as a boxplot per decade. Choosing between those drawings is that session’s lesson.
